chunks: Body diode in the off state, SW waveform. The question: What happens to the internal body diode in the off state? Draw the switch node voltage waveform.
During the buck's off state, the inductor current flows through the bottom transistor. But for a short dead time after the top one turns off, neither transistor is on.
The current then flows through the bottom transistor's built-in body diode, which pulls the switch node about 0. 7 volts below ground.
Then the channel turns on and the node returns close to 0 volts.
Picture a relay baton pass where the first runner drops out before the second takes over. For a moment the baton must go through a narrow side door instead of the open track.
The side door is the body diode: it works, but it costs more effort, shown as a deeper dip below zero on the waveform.
During dead time both gates are low and SW sits near -0. 75 volts.
The current rises from ground through Q 2 's body diode (the diode drawn alongside Q 2 , anode at the source/ground, cathode at the drain/SW) into SW and the inductor.
SW must sit one diode drop below ground for this to happen.
Body diode: the diode that is part of every MOSFET, from source to drain. Dead time: the gap when both transistors are off. Switch node (SW): the node whose voltage we draw.
Forward drop: the voltage across a conducting diode, about 0. 7 volts for a body diode. Reverse recovery: the brief backward current when the diode switches off.
Say 2 amps flows in the inductor. During the 20 nanoseconds dead time, the body diode carries it and the switch node sits at about -0. 7 volts.
Then the low-side transistor turns on, and with 10 milliohms it drops 2 times 0. 01 equals 20 millivolts, so the node sits at -0. 02 volts.
Described in words, the waveform is a square wave from about 0 to the input voltage with a small negative shelf at each edge. That is the whole idea.
"In the off state the inductor current keeps flowing through the low side.
During the dead time both FETs are off, so it flows through the low-side body diode and SW sits about one diode drop, 0. 7 to 1 volts, below ground.
Then the low-side channel turns on and SW comes up to about minus I R DS(on) , tens of millivolts. Before the high side turns on there's another dead-time shelf.
When the high side turns on the diode is forced off through reverse recovery, SW rises to V in with ringing. During the on state the body diode just blocks V in ."
